title: Escrow and Tax Rails for Agent-Hired Humans
one_liner: The compliance and payment layer that lets software agents legally hire humans for judgment and real-world tasks: owner KYC, task-legality screening, escrow, worker classification and tax forms.
customer: Agent-framework developers and companies whose agents need on-call humans (verification, phone calls, notarisation, in-person checks), plus the workers doing the tasks. Take rate is 8-12%.
problem: Agent-to-human marketplaces are appearing (47jobs, Hirenewtalent.ai in the brief, and viral 'rent a human' sites in early 2026), but nobody is the clear payor, employer or liable party. Who issues 1099s, who is responsible if an agent sends someone to do something illegal or never pays, and how do workers avoid scams?
solution: An API plus MCP tool ('ask_human'): agents post tasks against funded escrow tied to a KYC'd human or company principal. A legality and safety classifier rejects risky tasks. Automatic tax forms and classification, dispute arbitration and two-sided reputation follow, with optional injury insurance for physical tasks.
why_now: Agent frameworks and MCP matured in 2025, agent-payment standards and stablecoin rails are being rolled out, and agent-run marketplaces are going viral. Regulators will demand a principal of record after the first scandal.
revenue_model: 8-12% take rate on tasks plus an insurance margin for physical work.
non_obvious_insight: The marketplace is cheap to clone. The moat is the principal-of-record and liability layer, which is what regulators and enterprise buyers will eventually require, so building the compliant rails first wins the boring middle.
first_30_days: Ship a minimal escrow API and MCP tool with 200 vetted workers in one niche (phone verification calls, document notarisation, local checks in 3 cities). Onboard 10 agent builders through Discord and HN and complete the first 500 paid tasks.

title: Fractional Operator for Tiny Private Water Systems
one_liner: A flat-fee compliance back office and operator-of-record for the mobile-home parks, small subdivisions and rural employers that own small water systems and are about to face PFAS testing in 2027.
customer: Owners of mobile-home parks, small private water companies and HOA systems, and rural employers or private schools with their own wells. These are community and non-transient non-community systems, typically under 3,300 people. The owner is often an aging individual or family LLC with no operations staff.
problem: Owners face initial PFAS monitoring in 2027 and a 4.0 ppt limit still on the books. EPA's May 2026 proposal would move compliance from 2029 to 2031 and drop limits on four other compounds. The lead action level tightens on Nov 1, 2027. The whiplash freezes capex. Nobody at the business knows the sampling calendar, the accredited lab, the state portal, or the money ($1B of IIJA earmarked for PFAS testing and treatment, $7.2B of FY2026 SRF). The owner also cannot sell, because a first sample becomes a disclosure.
solution: Wedge: a $1,500 flat 'PFAS-2027 Readiness Pack' covering the sampling plan, lab coordination, result interpretation against 4.0 ppt, state filing and an options memo (treat, interconnect, drill, or sell). Upsell to a $600/mo retainer for the sampling calendar, consumer confidence report, lead inventory, monthly operator logs, tenant submetered billing and bookkeeping for a segregated water fund. The operator-of-record role is subcontracted to a state-certified operator partner. Later, broker and operate systems whose owners want out.
why_now: EPA's May 2026 proposals to delay PFAS compliance and rescind four limits have left small owners paralyzed, while 2027 initial monitoring still stands. Public money is earmarked: $1B IIJA for PFAS, $7.2B FY2026 SRF, and states are pushing consolidation of non-viable systems. The Boomer ownership wave is hitting the same long tail of tiny systems. EPA's science office was eliminated in 2026, so owners get less federal guidance.
revenue_model: $1,500 Readiness Pack. $400-$900/mo retainer per system by size. 6% success fee on SRF or state grants won. 2-4% brokerage fee on systems sold, plus an option to acquire orphan systems at distressed multiples using consolidation money.
non_obvious_insight: Federal delay does not remove the liability that appears at the first sample. Once a 2027 result exists it becomes a disclosure item in any sale, loan or insurance renewal. So the smart small owner samples early and under a plan. The firm that holds the compliance record becomes the natural buyer of last resort for a long tail of systems too small for the big acquirers. The retainer is the cheapest way to source those succession deals.
first_30_days: Sign one retired state-certified operator as partner and one accredited PFAS lab for a bulk rate. Join two state manufactured-housing associations and the state rural water association. Run free 'is my system covered?' webinars. Sell 10 Readiness Packs at $1,500 in one state, and use the results to prep 3 grant applications. Start compliance-only and add operator-of-record after the partner clears state rules.

title: Audit-Proof Records for CDL Training Schools
one_liner: A compliance layer that captures entry-level driver training records as training happens, so legitimate CDL school owners survive FMCSA registry purges and audits.
customer: Owners of independent CDL and truck driving schools (roughly 10-500 students a year), whose business depends on staying on FMCSA's Training Provider Registry.
problem: FMCSA has removed thousands of training providers from the registry, put thousands more on notice, and is running in-person audits of roughly 1,500 providers, with Justice Department and DHS attention to fraud in the CDL pipeline. Legitimate small schools with sloppy paperwork (instructor qualifications, curriculum hours, facility and vehicle documentation, timely completion uploads) can lose registration overnight. Students can't test, and the business dies.
solution: A mobile-first record system used on the range and in the classroom. QR or biometric check-in per session, driving-hour and behind-the-wheel logs, instructor qualification and expiry tracking, curriculum completion mapped to the ELDT requirements, and automatic, timely uploads to the registry. It produces an audit binder on demand, runs a mock audit, and offers an audit-day support line.
why_now: The FMCSA crackdown on training providers escalated through 2025-26, and 2026 in-person audits give failing providers about 30 days to fix problems before removal. Owners are frightened, and law firms and generic compliance tools aren't built for a 3-truck school in a strip mall. Carriers increasingly ask where new hires trained.
revenue_model: $299-799 per school per month depending on size. $1,500-3,000 for a one-time audit-readiness package or mock audit. A carrier-paid fee to verify graduates from a 'clean records' school network.
non_obvious_insight: An audit is a documentation exercise, and most schools that fail are honest but disorganized. The registry is a public, scrapeable list, so you can sell to every provider directly by name. Over time the audit-clean data lets you build a trusted graduate-verification network that carriers pay to hire from, which is a bigger business than compliance software alone.
first_30_days: Scrape the public Training Provider Registry list for two or three states. Cold-call and email owners with a free 20-point audit-readiness checklist. Sell a $1,500 audit-readiness package to the first 10 schools. Use their pain points to specify the mobile check-in and logging MVP.

title: RouteRx: Pharmacy Delivery on Co-op Fuel Routes
one_liner: Piggyback prescription and essentials delivery onto the propane, fuel and feed routes that already pass most rural households, so surviving independent pharmacies can serve people the chains just abandoned.
customer: Independent rural pharmacies (per-delivery fee), Medicare Advantage and Part D plans and rural health clinics (per-member adherence and wellness-check fee), and the co-op energy department, which keeps a share of route revenue.
problem: Rite Aid is gone, Walgreens is closing about 1,200 stores through 2027, and more than 2,000 US pharmacies closed in 2025 alone. Rural residents, especially older ones on propane and well water, are hours from a counter. Standalone courier delivery in a county of 12,000 people costs $15 to $30 a drop in deadhead miles. Independents cannot afford it, and plans cannot buy adherence in places with no last mile.
solution: The co-op's energy drivers already pass nearly every farmstead and acreage in a 25-mile radius on weekly or monthly cycles. They know the gate codes, where the dog is, and which customers live alone. Add a locked, tamper-evident tote and a driver app with signature capture and temperature logging. A partner pharmacy dispenses, and the driver acts as its contracted courier under existing Iowa delivery rules, with no controlled substances at first. Add optional 'no-heat and welfare check' notes that flag when a propane customer looks unwell, triggering a call to family or the clinic.
why_now: The 2025 to 2026 pharmacy shakeout has left rural pharmacy deserts, and Drug Channels' August 2026 analysis describes a K-shaped market of urban consolidation and rural lost access. Payers are looking for adherence and social-needs benefits. Co-op energy departments are under margin pressure and need new route revenue.
revenue_model: $5 to $9 per delivery from pharmacies. Medicare Advantage and Part D plan per-member-per-month adherence and check-in fees. The co-op takes a route revenue share of roughly 30%. Optional expansion to labs, groceries and parcels.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing in rural health is not delivery technology but route density that is already paid for. A propane bobtail passing a home every three weeks has a near-zero marginal stop cost, and it carries something no courier startup has, which is trust from decades of showing up.
first_30_days: Sign one co-op with an LP fleet and one independent pharmacy in an adjacent town that just lost a competitor. Get a written read from the Iowa Board of Pharmacy and the co-op's insurer. Run a 20-household pilot with tamper-evident bags and an off-the-shelf delivery app. Record cost per stop and refill adherence to pitch a regional Medicare Advantage plan.

title: Infection-Safe Energy Retrofits for Animal Shelters
one_liner: A shared-savings energy contractor that designs heat-recovery ventilation, heat pumps and batteries around shelter-medicine infection-control rules, funded by pet-welfare philanthropy and paid partly by utility resilience programs.
customer: Animal shelters, humane societies, boarding and daycare facilities and 24-hour emergency vet hospitals. Funders include pet-welfare foundations and utilities. The buyer is the shelter director or board, and the payers are philanthropy plus shared savings.
problem: Shelters must move a lot of conditioned air (guidelines commonly call for roughly 10-20 air changes per hour) to control respiratory disease, run heavy laundry and hot-water loads 24/7, and cannot go dark in a heat wave or outage. Utility rates rose 7.3% in a year. Most are nonprofits in old buildings, and energy contractors either cut ventilation (raising disease risk) or refuse the job. Meanwhile pet philanthropy is arriving but is aimed at care, not capex (Duffield's $250M over 5 years starts with 250 x $10K grants).
solution: A standard package built around air-change and zoning constraints: energy-recovery ventilation, heat pump water heaters for laundry, right-sized battery and optional solar with a critical-load panel. It is financed by grants, utility rebates, elective-pay tax credits where still eligible (to be verified per project) and shared savings. Shelters also commit to serve as pet-inclusive cooling or warming refuge in emergencies, with a utility or city paying an availability fee.
why_now: Duffield's $250M commitment (September 17, 2026) and PetSmart Charities' $100M pledge put unprecedented money into shelters. Electricity prices, storage costs (about $70/kWh packs) and utility resilience programs make small batteries viable, and no vendor has encoded shelter-medicine ventilation rules.
revenue_model: Design and project-management fee of 8-12% on $60-250K retrofits, plus a 20-30% share of verified savings for 7-10 years on projects financed by grant or green-loan capital, plus utility or city availability payments for refuge capacity.
non_obvious_insight: The binding constraint in a shelter is infection control, not kWh. The first vendor that treats ventilation and cross-contamination as design rules owns a trusted niche, and philanthropy has cash but no capex vehicle for energy.
first_30_days: Offer 10 shelters free utility-bill audits and publish an anonymized shelter energy benchmark. Help 3 of them use first-round philanthropic grants to fund detailed audits. Close one small paid project (heat pump water heaters for laundry) to build a case study. Talk to two utilities about a refuge availability payment.

title: Assisted Short Sales for Underwater Auto Loans
one_liner: Record auto originations lead to record delinquencies and a repossession glut. Give lenders a mortgage-style short sale for cars that recovers more than auction does.
customer: Credit unions and subprime and indirect auto lenders with rising 60-plus-day delinquencies.
problem: Auto originations hit a record $211B and auto delinquencies also hit a record (CNBC and others, Aug 2026). Lenders' only tool at scale is repossession and auction, which is slow, costly and yields discounted recoveries. Borrowers keep a deficiency balance and wrecked credit, and lenders lose more than a cooperative sale would cost them.
solution: At 45-60 days delinquent, the lender offers the borrower a lender-blessed voluntary sale. The platform lists the car at retail to dealers and private buyers, handles payoff letters, title and lien release in each state, and converts the shortfall into a small structured note or forgiveness within lender-set limits. The lender pays only when its net recovery beats projected repo loss.
why_now: Delinquencies at records, auction supply pressure, and credit unions with growing delinquent books and a reputation to protect. Mortgage short-sale playbooks are well understood, but nobody has ported them to autos.
revenue_model: Flat fee (about $500-$700) or 3-5% of sale price per completed sale, plus a performance share of recovery improvement over projected repo loss.
non_obvious_insight: Lenders already lose money on repossession, but their servicing, collections and legal workflows are built around it, so no infrastructure exists to choreograph title, payoff and buyer across 50 states. The product is that plumbing.
first_30_days: Partner with two or three credit unions with 5k-plus delinquent auto loans. Run a manual pilot in one state with a small dealer buyer network, comparing net recovery per unit against actual auction results. Use the data to sign a master services agreement.

title: Pre-Loss Home Reconstruction Dossiers for Insurance Claims
one_liner: Rebuild, in the exact quality and condition language insurers can't wave away, what a destroyed home actually had, using old appraisals, listing photos, permits and imagery.
customer: Public adjusters and policyholder-side insurance attorneys handling total-loss wildfire, hurricane and tornado claims pay $900-2,500 per dossier. Direct-to-homeowner is $495 for a basic version. Independent insurance agents later buy a 'pre-loss baseline' for their high-value clients.
problem: After a total loss, the insurer's estimate assumes builder-grade finishes and smaller square footage. The survivor's photos and receipts burned, so 'like kind and quality' becomes a memory-versus-spreadsheet fight worth tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars per house. Public adjusters reconstruct from Zillow photos and homeowner recollection, which adjusters on the other side discount.
solution: A retrospective, signed 'as-was' dossier delivered in about 5 business days. Sources: (1) any prior purchase or refinance appraisal the homeowner has (borrowers are entitled to copies) or can get through the lender or servicer; (2) archived MLS photos and remarks from the last sale; (3) permit and remodel history; (4) assessor quality and size records; (5) historical aerial and street-level imagery. A licensed appraiser assigns the standard Q1-Q6 quality and C1-C6 condition ratings, lists the finishes and features, and estimates replacement cost at that quality level.
why_now: The January 2025 Los Angeles fires destroyed roughly 16,000 structures, and many claims are still being contested in late 2026. Every wildfire and hurricane season adds more total losses. Insurers are tightening costs and leaning on adjuster software. Photo and record archives from prior sales are now digital and searchable, so the reconstruction is a 5-day job.
revenue_model: Flat fee per dossier only. USPAP forbids contingent appraisal fees, and independence is the product's credibility. Volume pricing for public adjuster firms. $99/yr 'baseline vault' (current LiDAR, photos and Q/C ratings) sold through independent insurance agents in wildfire and hurricane zones, who carry E&O exposure when clients are underinsured.
non_obvious_insight: The best pre-loss evidence in America already exists, sitting in lender closing files, appraisal workfiles kept five years and old MLS pages. Nobody connects it to claims. A neutral licensed appraiser's dated interior photos and Q/C ratings carry far more weight with an insurer than a homeowner's testimony. Those disputes are won at the finish level (cabinetry, flooring, millwork), not on square footage, and the appraiser's rating vocabulary is what claims examiners recognize.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 appraisers in Los Angeles County who lost work. Build one dossier template. Offer 5 free pilot dossiers to 2-3 public adjuster firms and one policyholder attorney working Altadena or Pacific Palisades cases, and measure how much the insurer's revised offer moves. Then charge $1,500 per dossier and use the measured lift as the sales pitch.

title: Security Grant Desk for Small Congregations
one_liner: Flat-fee application, vulnerability-assessment and post-award compliance packages for small houses of worship using FEMA's Nonprofit Security Grant Program and state equivalents.
customer: Small synagogues, mosques, churches, gurdwaras and temples, and umbrella bodies such as federations, dioceses and mosque councils.
problem: FY2026 NSGP offered $300M (notice published 24 June 2026, deadline extended to 24 July) at up to $200k per site. Applications need a vulnerability assessment, an investment justification and SAM.gov and UEI registration. Small congregations lack the administrative capacity, and post-award procurement and reimbursement rules trip them.
solution: Templated assessments built on CISA's free self-assessment, an investment-justification drafting workflow with security-vendor quote gathering, SAM and UEI onboarding, a state-agency deadline tracker, and post-award procurement and reimbursement compliance. Flat fees only, because FEMA guidance generally bars contingent-fee grant writing.
why_now: FY2026 awards are being announced now and FY2027 prep starts this fall. Threat levels keep congregations motivated.
revenue_model: $1.5-4k per application, $800 for post-award compliance, and $150/month trackers for federations.
non_obvious_insight: The barrier is administrative capacity, not eligibility, and referrals flow through community federations. Post-award compliance is the neglected second revenue stream.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 regional federations or mosque councils, run free FY2027-prep webinars, and sell 10 assessment packages. Build a network of vetted security installers for quotes.

title: AI Chat-History Exposure Assessments for Breach Counsel
one_liner: When infostealers grab employees' AI sessions, tell breach counsel what the attacker could actually have read and whether notification is triggered.
customer: Incident-response boutiques, privacy and breach law firms, cyber-insurer panel vendors, and enterprise DPOs. Priced per incident.
problem: Infostealer logs exposed AI sessions tied to 80,000+ corporate domains, and 358 of 482 large companies analyzed had stolen ChatGPT/OpenAI sessions. A stolen session is a searchable archive of contracts, source code, and personal data, and it bypasses MFA. IR tooling was built for mailboxes and file shares, so nobody can say whether an AI-history breach triggers legal notification.
solution: Ingest infostealer-feed hits mapped to employee AI accounts. Combine them with the customer's enterprise export or compliance-API data to classify the sampled chats after the theft window by data class (PII, PHI, credentials, deal information, source code). Deliver a notification-decision memo, an affected-person list, remediation steps (session revocation, key rotation), and an insurer-ready timeline.
why_now: The 2026 infostealer data shows stolen AI sessions at scale. Enterprise AI adoption now puts sensitive work in chat, and insurers are adding AI exclusions, so they want scoping evidence before paying.
revenue_model: $5-25K per incident, with $1-2K per month monitoring retainers and channel referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: The breach is not the stolen cookie but the content behind it, and notification law turns on data, not credentials. No tool in the IR stack handles AI transcripts, so a small team can own the category before platform vendors bother.
first_30_days: Sign 3 IR boutiques as channel partners. Build a classification pipeline over enterprise chat exports. Run the first paid assessments at a $7.5K flat fee using hits from commercial infostealer-intel feeds.

title: Home-Readiness Crews for Hospital-at-Home Programs
one_liner: On-call crews that make a patient's home hospital-ready in hours and provide a non-clinical overnight presence for the first 72 hours.
customer: Hospital-at-Home program directors at health systems, and Medicare Advantage plans and ACOs that fund them.
problem: Extending the waiver lets programs scale, but many referred patients get screened out because of clutter, stairs, pets, bad Wi-Fi or power, no bedside space, or no adult present overnight. Every screen-out is a lost admission that would have replaced $2,500+ inpatient days. No one owns the home itself.
solution: A van and two-person crew does a rapid home assessment (power, connectivity via hotspot or eSIM, safe path, bedside setup, hazard removal, DME handoff). A vetted sitter provides overnight presence and escalates to the nurse line, and the crew resets the home at discharge. An address-based readiness score pre-screens referrals before the ED sends them.
why_now: The Hospital-at-Home waiver was extended five years, to Sep 30, 2030, so systems are committing capital and hiring. 80+ growth and 90% occupancy in senior housing mean more frail patients whose homes are the constraint.
revenue_model: Per-episode fee of $350-900 plus monthly retainers for guaranteed response, and a software license for the readiness score.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource isn't clinicians or tech; it's a safe physical environment and a body in the room at 3 am. Whoever solves 'make the home hospital-grade' raises hospital-at-home conversion rates, which is what programs are judged on.
first_30_days: Pitch three hospital-at-home directors and offer a pilot at cost on 20 episodes, using existing local caregiver and sitter pools. Track screen-out conversion and cost per episode.

title: Craft Data: Retiring Machinists Teach Robots
one_liner: Pay shops to let experienced craftspeople wear cameras and gloves, and sell the captured factory-floor skill data to robot-learning labs.
customer: Robot foundation-model and humanoid companies buying training data. Shops are the second customer, receiving cash and auto-generated standard work instructions.
problem: Physical AI funding hit $18.6B in Q2 2026, but labs lack high-quality real-world industrial manipulation data (setups, fixturing, deburring, measuring by feel). Meanwhile a retiring workforce takes unrecorded tacit skill, and no dataset of it exists.
solution: An egocentric capture kit (head and wrist cameras, instrumented glove, audio narration) worn during normal work. Add job context from CAM programs and travelers. Deliver curated, annotated datasets to labs. Shops receive setup videos, SOPs and a training library, and workers share in revenue, with consent, IP and safety protocols agreed up front.
why_now: Record physical-AI funding, cheap wearable capture hardware, imitation-learning advances, and a retirement wave. Labs need real industrial data, not lab data.
revenue_model: Target $150-400 per curated hour from labs (to validate with first buyers). Pay shops about $40 an hour. $500 a month per shop for the SOP and training library.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input to robot learning is expertise, not compute. The same footage is a shop's best defense against retirement knowledge loss, so shops will host the capture and even pay for the by-product.
first_30_days: Recruit five shops with free SOP videos as the hook. Capture 100 hours. Pitch five labs with samples. Aim for one paid pilot of $20-50k. Hire an employment lawyer for consent and IP terms.

title: Biotech Graveyard Data Exchange
one_liner: Rescue, clean and license the wet-lab data of shutting-down biotechs, especially the failed and negative results that AI drug-discovery models are starved of, and split the proceeds with the estate.
customer: AI-drug-discovery companies, big-pharma computational groups and ML-for-bio labs that license proprietary training data (ADME/tox, assay panels, SAR series, structural data). The sellers are wind-down estates, VCs and founders, who get a revenue share instead of paying anything.
problem: After the 2022-2025 biotech funding drought, hundreds of venture-backed biotechs have shut down or been hollowed out. When the last employee leaves, years of proprietary experimental data die on unpaid cloud accounts, expired ELN and LIMS licenses and laptops. Meanwhile AI models are trained on published literature, which is survivorship-biased: negative results almost never get published. Models lack the data on what does not work, and that data is exactly what dead companies hold.
solution: A wind-down data-salvage service, done in a 60-day window between the last payroll and server deletion. Triage what data exists and what is encumbered (licensor and CRO rights, academic-license terms). Extract from ELN, LIMS, instruments and cloud buckets. Limit the first scope to non-human-subject data such as biochemical and cell assays, chemistry, DMPK and structural data, so there is no PII problem. Get IP and rights sign-off from the estate or assignee. Standardize to a common assay schema with provenance. License as curated bundles to AI-bio and pharma buyers, with revenue flowing back to the estate.
why_now: The biotech shutdown and reverse-merger wave is in full swing, with wind-down specialists and startup shutdown services now established. AI-bio companies and pharma are openly competing for proprietary data, including federated and data-for-model-access programs. The 23andMe data-in-bankruptcy episode showed how badly data is currently handled in wind-downs. Cheap LLM-assisted schema mapping now makes normalizing messy legacy assay data affordable.
revenue_model: Free or low-cost triage for the estate. Take 30-50% of licensing revenue on each bundle, plus a fixed curation fee charged to buyers. Later, sell subscription access to a growing pooled 'negative results' corpus organized by target class.
non_obvious_insight: The dataset with the most scarcity value is the one everyone considers worthless: failed programs. Sellers are motivated because the alternative is deletion, and there is no consumer-privacy problem in assay data, unlike almost every other 'data for AI' market. The moat is trust and presence at the exact moment a company dies, meaning relationships with wind-down lawyers, biotech VCs and CFO-for-hire networks, not technology.
first_30_days: Reach out to 20 biotech VC platform partners, wind-down lawyers and fractional CFOs with a one-page offer of free data triage, revenue share and zero cost to the estate. Sign 2-3 shutting-down biotechs. Pre-sell sample packs to 3-5 AI-bio buyers and get a letter of intent on price per curated dataset. Build the minimal schema-normalization pipeline on the first dataset and get legal templates for estate-to-exchange licensing. Ship the first licensed bundle within the first 2-3 months.

title: Global Rain Radar From Starlink Dishes
one_liner: Turn opted-in Starlink terminals into the densest rain-gauge network ever built and sell ground-truth rainfall to insurers.
customer: Parametric crop and flood insurers and MGAs, reinsurers, agricultural cooperatives, utilities and municipal flood teams.
problem: Rain gauges are sparse and radar coverage is poor in rural and developing regions. Parametric insurance suffers from basis risk, and disputes arise when the index does not match what happened at the field.
solution: An open-source agent reads a terminal's local signal telemetry, correlates rain-induced attenuation with rain rate, and produces minute-level hyperlocal rainfall. Owners opt in and receive a monthly credit. Sell the result as an API and as audited trigger data for parametric products.
why_now: Starlink reached 12M subscribers, including many rural users. The idea of using satellite-link attenuation as a rain sensor is established in research. Parametric insurance is growing, and public radar and gauge budgets are under pressure.
revenue_model: API subscriptions $20-200k per year per insurer or cooperative. Per-trigger data fees. Owner credits of $2-5 per month as the cost of goods.
non_obvious_insight: Rain fade is a nuisance to network engineers but a measurement to meteorologists. The sensors are already installed and paid for by their owners.
first_30_days: Adapt open-source telemetry tools and recruit 300 terminal owners with a small credit. Co-locate with 30 tipping-bucket gauges and publish a validation note. Pitch two parametric MGAs and one agricultural cooperative, and plan a fallback if SpaceX restricts local access.

title: Proctored Truth Audits for School Edtech
one_liner: Short, paper-based, device-free probes that tell districts whether the practice software they license teaches anything, now that AI can do the practice for the child.
customer: District curriculum and assessment directors (5k-50k student districts) that renew six-figure math/ELA practice licenses; secondary: charter networks. Edtech vendors are a later, firewalled buyer of verified listings.
problem: Practice dashboards show rising accuracy, but ALEKS data (June 2026 working paper, not peer-reviewed) show proctored word-problem accuracy falling from about 80% to about 60% after ChatGPT while unsupervised accuracy rose. A 2-year Tennessee study found Khanmigo added nothing over Khan Academy alone. Districts renew on usage and mastery metrics that AI now contaminates.
solution: Twenty-minute proctored paper probes at the start, middle and end of term, on a random sample of classrooms, aligned to the same standards as the platform and including graphing items that are hard to paste into AI. Human-scored from scans. Output is a per-product, per-school report: what share of platform 'mastery' survives an unassisted check, and cost per verified mastery. Later, a benchmark vendors pay to be listed on.
why_now: Unsupervised practice data has visibly decoupled from learning (2026 ALEKS study). ESSER money is gone, so renewals get scrutiny. NYC and LAUSD paused AI for 2026-27, and boards now want proof. Over half of teachers say AI harms critical thinking.
revenue_model: Annual district audit contracts of $15k-60k per product per grade band, plus per-school scanning and scoring fees. Later, vendor-funded verification listings kept separate from the audit results.
non_obvious_insight: When students can outsource practice, engagement and accuracy metrics measure the AI, not the child. The only trustworthy learning data is now scarce, unassisted and physical, so the measurement layer, not the content layer, becomes the moat.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 curriculum directors who are mid-renewal fight. Run a free 6-classroom pilot with paper probes built from released state-test items plus hand-drawn graphing items. Have a few retired teachers score them. Hand over a 2-page usage-versus-learning report before their renewal decision, then convert to a $15-25k paid audit.

title: Closure-as-a-Service for Colleges and Grad Programs
one_liner: Orchestrating orderly teach-outs, transcript custody and student transfers for shutting colleges and graduate programs that the new loan caps and demographics are about to gut.
customer: Small private colleges and graduate programs facing closure or merger, state higher-ed regulators, accreditors, and university systems absorbing programs.
problem: The enrollment cliff plus the end of Grad PLUS and the new caps push small colleges and grad programs (nursing, counseling and others) below viability. Closures are chaotic: teach-out agreements, records custody, transfer-credit mapping, refunds and student communications are improvised, and regulators and accreditors demand teach-out plans.
solution: A standing playbook, software and partner network: pre-negotiated teach-out partners, an AI-assisted transfer-credit mapper across receiving schools, secure transcript and records custody, student communications, and tracking of closure obligations. Sell a 'teach-out readiness audit' and retainer to at-risk institutions before they need it.
why_now: The July 2026 aid reset, K-12 and college demographic cliffs and rising closures make this a recurring workload. State regulators are searching for standard processes.
revenue_model: $20-50k annual readiness retainers, $100-400k per closure project, $5-15 per student per year records custody, and referral fees from receiving institutions.
non_obvious_insight: Institutions treat closure as a one-time catastrophe, but with hundreds at risk it is a recurring, standardizable service, like a bankruptcy trustee, where fees come from the estate and reputation for orderly process determines who gets hired.
first_30_days: Publish a teach-out readiness checklist. Offer a $7.5k readiness audit to 10 small colleges and 2 state regulators. Recruit an ex-registrar and an ex-accreditation consultant as delivery leads.

title: Rent Renewal Desk for Small Tenants
one_liner: Contingency-fee lease-renewal negotiation for tenants under 5,000 square feet, armed with the comps and lease abstraction that landlords get from CoStar-class data and small tenants never see.
customer: Independent restaurants, salons, clinics, small offices and shops with leases expiring in 6 to 18 months. Channels: bookkeepers and CPAs, POS providers and merchant associations.
problem: Landlords and their brokers negotiate with professional comps and lease abstracts, while small tenants negotiate blind. Tenant-rep brokers skip small deals because the commission is too small, so owners accept the renewal escalator, the personal guarantee and CAM charges by default. Crowdsourced comp platforms such as CompStak sell to brokers and investors, not to a florist with a lease renewal.
solution: The tenant uploads the lease and the last 12 months of CAM invoices. The desk builds a comp set (public deeds, listing asking rents, pooled tenant-contributed leases, licensed broker data), then returns a one-page 'you pay X% over or under market' report plus a negotiation script and draft letter. An optional we-negotiate tier uses a licensed broker partner, and a CAM audit is an upsell. Renewal alerts fire 18 months before expiry.
why_now: LLM document extraction can now abstract a 60-page lease and CAM reconciliation in minutes at a cost of cents, work that used to cost a lawyer $500 to $1,500. Tariff and wage pressure has made rent the last fixed cost small operators can still attack. CompStak's give-to-get model shows lease data can be crowdsourced when contributors get something back.
revenue_model: A $149 fair-rent report. 20% to 25% of first-year rent savings for full negotiation. 25% contingency on CAM overcharges recovered. Bookkeeper and association referral revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: Information asymmetry is total at the small end, and the professionals who could close it are priced out by deal size. AI cuts the cost of a competent negotiation to a few hours. The lasting moat is a pooled, tenant-owned lease database, because landlords' data is proprietary but tenants' data is scattered and freely contributed if they get their own comps back.
first_30_days: Offer a free fair-rent check to 50 businesses in one dense commercial corridor through two local bookkeepers and a merchants' association. Build the lease-abstraction pipeline and a first comp set from the leases collected. Close five contingency negotiations, measure realized savings, and use the results as the sales deck for the next 100 tenants.

title: Tariff Refund Liquidation-Cliff Radar
one_liner: A deadline tracker and filing generator for small importers and small customs brokers that tells them, entry by entry, which refund route is still open and when it closes.
customer: Importers with 200-20,000 entries per year, and independent customs brokers serving them, who lack in-house trade counsel. Priced per entry or as a success fee.
problem: CBP will not refund automatically. Filers must act through CAPE, a Post Summary Correction (PSC) or a protest, and each route has a different window. CAPE Phase 1 accepts only unliquidated entries or entries liquidated in the preceding 80 days. Protests must be filed within 180 days of liquidation. PSCs must be filed within 300 days of entry or 15 days before liquidation. Finally liquidated entries, drawback, TIB and reconciliation entries are ineligible. The importer also needs ACE Portal access and ACH enrollment on file. Any outstanding CBP debt is offset first under 19 CFR 24.72.
solution: The tool ingests the ACE entry summary and liquidation reports (ES-003 or ES-022 exports, or a broker CSV). It assigns every IEEPA-duty entry a status and route (CAPE-eligible now, protest-only, PSC window, ineligible) and a hard 'last day' date. It auto-builds CAPE declaration files (up to 9,999 entries) for the broker and protest packets for the rest. It reconciles ACH deposits and interest against the ACE refund reports (REV-603 and REV-615) so the finance team can book the refund entry by entry. It flags CBP-debt offsets and scam solicitations, since CBP has warned about fraudsters targeting refund claimants.
why_now: The rolling cliff is live. Every month another vintage of 2025 entries liquidates, and each has a fresh 80-day CAPE window and a 180-day protest window that can lapse silently. Refunds are being recognised in one lump. AutoZone's alone was worth $4.43 EPS in a quarter. Auditors will require entry-level tie-outs.
revenue_model: $3-8 per entry tracked, $25K-$75K annual site licences for small brokers with 50+ importer clients, or a 3-5% success fee on refunds recovered from entries that would otherwise have gone finally liquidated.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is a calendar, not law-firm expertise. CBP's own pages say 'ACE accepts CAPE Declarations containing entries liquidated within the preceding 80 days', 'once an entry has liquidated, a protest may be filed within 180 days', and 'you cannot remove entries from the Declaration' once filed (https://www.cbp.gov/trade/programs-administration/trade-remedies/ieepa-duty-refunds and https://www.cbp.gov/trade/programs-administration/trade-remedies/IEEPA-FAQ). CBP says only the IOR or its broker can file, and the FAQ never mentions automatic refunds. Public companies are already booking eight-figure refunds (AutoZone about $96M, MillerKnoll $16.5M, Worthington $4M: https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/23/worthington-wor-q1-2027-earnings-call-transcript/). The long tail of small importers is running on broker email chains and is the most likely to lose entries to a missed window.
first_30_days: Cold-email and call 100 independent customs brokers (from NCBFAA and local port broker lists) with an offer: 'send us your entry list and we'll return a route-and-deadline sheet within 24 hours, free'. Build the classifier in a spreadsheet plus a Python script. Publish a public liquidation-date calculator as a lead magnet aimed at importers. Convert the first 3 brokers to a paid per-entry contract, and have each refer 5-10 importer clients.

title: Data-Center Community Benefits That Fund Rural Vets
one_liner: An intermediary that packages animal-care compacts (vet loan repayment, mobile clinics, low-cost care days, shelter energy upgrades) as community-benefit commitments for data-center developers fighting local opposition.
customer: Data-center developers and hyperscaler community-affairs teams siting campuses in rural and exurban counties, plus county officials. Payment is a program management fee on the pledged benefit package.
problem: Seven in ten Americans oppose data centers in their community (Gallup) and New York has imposed a statewide hyperscale moratorium. Delays are extremely costly (a delayed 60 MW commissioning costs about $14M a month). Typical community benefits are abstract (tax revenue, school grants). Meanwhile rural counties face a vet shortage (91,100 US vets, only about 3,100 openings a year) and vet costs are the single most visible affordability pressure for pet and livestock owners.
solution: Design and run a neutral 'Vet Access Compact' per county: loan repayment or salary top-ups for rural vets and techs, a solar-battery mobile clinic, quarterly low-cost vaccine and spay/neuter days, and shelter energy upgrades. Administer it with measurable outcomes (appointments, wait times), match it with philanthropic dollars where possible, and give the developer credible, publishable reporting. Optionally link the developer's backup power to the clinic's resilience.
why_now: Data-center opposition and moratoria surged in 2026, and electricity affordability is a midterm issue. Duffield's $250M commitment and PetSmart Charities' pledge provide matching money. New vet-professional tiers (Colorado's VPA) expand who can be funded.
revenue_model: 10-15% program design and administration fee on $1-5M multi-year packages, grant-matching and outcome-reporting retainers, and implementation fees for mobile clinics.
non_obvious_insight: Animals are one of the few bipartisan, hyper-local issues that reach every county, and a $2M program is a rounding error against a $1B campus. It pairs capital-rich, trust-poor developers with trust-rich, capital-poor local vets who also speak at public hearings.
first_30_days: Pick 3 counties with pending data-center hearings on the public calendar. Call the county veterinary association and extension office to map the gaps. Produce a one-page compact and pitch it to developers' community-affairs leads. Sell a $15-30K design study as the first paid engagement. Avoid contingent fees tied to permit outcomes.

title: Pooled Radiation Test Data for Commercial Chips
one_liner: A subscription database and beam-time broker so satellite builders stop each paying to test the same commercial chips.
customer: Constellation and smallsat builders using commercial parts, defense new-space suppliers, and chip vendors seeking space design wins.
problem: Proliferated constellations (Golden Dome's reported 600-satellite award, Starlink) run on commercial parts. Radiation-beam slots are scarce with multi-month queues, and results live in silos. Roughly the same popular parts get tested repeatedly.
solution: Pool member orders to buy block beam time at university and national facilities, and test the top parts by lot and date code. Publish a member-contributed database of results and anomalies, and broker custom tests. Members trade their data for access.
why_now: Defense demand for proliferated LEO and a wave of well-funded satellite makers are stressing limited test capacity. Commercial-parts-first design is now standard.
revenue_model: $10-50k per year per member. 10-15% fee on brokered custom tests. Sponsored testing from chip vendors.
non_obvious_insight: In a commercial-parts space industry, test data is the scarce asset, not the parts. The group that pools it becomes the standards-setter.
first_30_days: Contact two beam facilities about block-time pricing. Pre-sell five founding memberships to satellite builders at $10k each. Publish a free first report on one popular microcontroller or memory part to establish credibility.

title: Disposable Ocean Drifters Reporting Through Orbit
one_liner: $10-30 drifting sensors dropped from passing ships that report through Bluetooth-to-satellite links, building a dense ocean nowcast.
customer: Weather-routing companies, offshore wind and energy operators, hurricane-season shipping and fishing fleets, insurers and coast guards.
problem: Ocean observation is sparse and expensive, because standard buoys cost thousands of dollars each, and some public observing networks have reportedly lost capacity. Routing and offshore-operations customers pay for better current, wave and sea-surface data.
solution: A disposable floating sensor (GPS, temperature, basic wave motion) that uses a standard Bluetooth chip and a Bluetooth-to-satellite network for uplink. Recruit ships of opportunity (research vessels, yacht races, cargo lines) to deploy hundreds. Sell a nowcast layer and event-specific coverage such as hurricane drifts.
why_now: Hubble Network (6 satellites, $200M Series C) shows ordinary Bluetooth chips can reach orbit, and its next generation improves link margins. Sensors and uplink are now cheap enough for disposable use.
revenue_model: Data subscriptions $20-100k per year per routing or offshore customer. Event campaigns of $50-200k. Sensor kits sold at cost to research and racing fleets.
non_obvious_insight: Cheap satellite uplink flips ocean sensing from a few expensive fixed buoys to millions of throwaway ones, and ships already crossing the ocean provide free deployment.
first_30_days: Build 50 prototype drifters and test the link at sea on a partner yacht or research cruise. Sign two weather-routing or offshore wind customers for paid pilots before the next hurricane season.

title: Robotaxi Escort: Curb-to-Exam-Room Concierge
one_liner: Trained escorts who meet seniors at the door, ride the robotaxi with them, wait at the appointment and bring them home, replacing costly NEMT vehicles.
customer: Medicare Advantage plans with transport benefits, adult children, life-plan communities and hospital discharge teams, at about $45-60 per escorted round trip.
problem: Robotaxis carry about 500k paid rides a week in 10+ metros, but a frail rider cannot handle the app, curb boarding or a walker, and cannot find the right entrance. Traditional non-emergency medical transport with vans and drivers costs $90-150 a trip and is unreliable.
solution: Unbundle NEMT. The autonomous car supplies the vehicle and the driver-free miles, and the escort supplies only the missing human parts: booking on the senior's behalf, door-through-door help, walker stowage, waiting and handoff to clinic staff. Family members receive live trip updates and fraud-safe spending limits.
why_now: Waymo is at about 3,900 vehicles with fares from Zoox starting Aug 2026. Seniors now hold Medicaid and MA transport benefits that plans want to cut costs on.
revenue_model: Per-trip fee ($45-60 escort plus ride cost passed through) or $199 a month family subscription. Gross margin of 35-45% after escort wages.
non_obvious_insight: Robotaxis remove the driver but not the need for a helper at each end. Whoever provides that helper owns the senior segment, and no fleet operator wants to.
first_30_days: Launch in one Waymo metro (Phoenix or Austin) with 10 escorts recruited from nursing students and retirees. Sign five independent-living communities and two geriatric clinics for private-pay trips. Then approach an MA plan's transport benefit team with trip logs.

title: Cross-Lender Double-Pledge Registry for Receivables
one_liner: A hashed, shared ledger where lenders confirm that an invoice, receivable or auto loan has not already been pledged elsewhere, starting with freight and trade factoring.
customer: Independent factoring companies, ABL desks at regional banks, supply-chain-finance funds and private-credit lenders to mid-market suppliers.
problem: First Brands allegedly double- and triple-pledged about $2.3B of invoices. The SEC charged Tricolor's former CEO and CFO on 18 Aug 2026 with double-pledging subprime auto loans to multiple lenders and securitisations. No single funder can detect overlap because there is no mechanism for lenders to see each other's pledges, so small factors are hit constantly.
solution: Members submit hashed invoice fingerprints (debtor ID, invoice number, amount, date) by API and get 'clean' or 'conflict' back in seconds. Add automated debtor confirmation (email, portal and EDI checks that the invoice exists and where payment is directed) and remittance-diversion alerts. Use private set intersection or salted hashes so lenders never reveal borrowers, and a consortium contract plus UCC-style notice.
why_now: First Brands and Tricolor collapsed in Sept 2025, and DOJ (Jan 2026) and SEC (Aug 2026) actions followed. Private credit's growth, investor demands for collateral verification and bar-association guidance on being 'two-timed' have created board-level urgency.
revenue_model: $0.10-2 per query, $1-5k per month membership for small factors, $50k+ per year for funds, and $5-15 per automated debtor confirmation.
non_obvious_insight: Fraud lives in the gaps between lenders, not inside them. The data everyone needs (each other's pledges) is data nobody will share bilaterally. A neutral registry sells a network effect for detection, like Carfax or the UK's Cifas, rather than a better anomaly detector.
first_30_days: Start with freight factoring, where duplicate invoices and fake brokers are a known problem. Sign 10 independent factors and two fintech ABL lenders through industry associations, build the hashing API, and offer founding members a free tier in exchange for contributing data.

title: Certified Scrap Kill for Aircraft Parts
one_liner: A mobile crew and app that destroys, photographs and certifies scrapped aircraft parts so they can never resurface as fake 'serviceable' parts, and sells the segregated metal.
customer: Regional airline stores and quality departments, Part 145 repair stations, lessors managing teardowns and part-outs, and engine and component shops. They pay a per-event fee, partly offset by a share of the alloy value.
problem: Every airline is supposed to mutilate parts that are beyond economical repair or time-expired so they cannot re-enter the supply chain. On the floor, the scrap cage gets emptied by a metals dealer on a handshake. Serial plates are sometimes cut off and sometimes not. Techs and stores people know that 'scrapped' units can turn up months later 'overhauled' at a broker with a tidy set of documents. The airline also carries the paper trail risk. If a fake part traces back to your serial number, you are in the investigation. Meanwhile titanium and nickel-alloy scrap is sold mixed at a low commodity price, because nobody segregates it.
solution: A van with a shear or plasma cutter, a tag punch and a phone app. Per drum or per pallet, the crew scans and photographs part number and serial number before destruction, destroys the part in a way that defeats reuse, photographs it again after, and pushes a hash-stamped certificate of destruction into the customer's inventory system. This removes the item from their books and gives quality staff and lessor auditors an unbroken chain of custody. Scrap is segregated by alloy and sold to specialty metal buyers, which funds the service.
why_now: Scrutiny of unapproved and counterfeit parts has stayed high since the 2023 forged-release-certificate scandal involving CFM56 parts. The FAA has long-standing guidance on detecting and reporting suspected unapproved parts (AC 21-29), and lessors and insurers keep tightening audit requirements. Fleet retirements of older regional aircraft in 2025-2026 are creating unusually large scrap volumes. Cheap phone-based photo and OCR capture removes the need for special hardware.
revenue_model: Fee per destruction event or per kilogram ($X per event plus a metal revenue share, typically netting near zero out of pocket for the airline). Annual chain-of-custody programs for lessors and MROs. Later, sell certified segregated alloy lots to aerospace melters at a premium.
non_obvious_insight: Airlines treat scrap as a solved cost center. Techs know it is the weakest link in traceability. The buyer's pain is not the cost of scrap, it is being named in the paper trail of a counterfeit. Whoever owns certified destruction owns a record that every auditor, lessor and regulator increasingly wants. The metal value pays for the service, so the airline's out-of-pocket is close to zero, and that removes the budget objection.
first_30_days: Choose one metro with a regional hub plus several 145 shops. Buy a used band saw or plasma cutter and a tag punch, and line up a metals dealer that will accept segregated alloys. Have an aviation attorney draft a certificate of destruction that cites the operator's own manual procedure and AC 21-29. Offer the first scrap-cage clear-out free to 3-5 quality managers, with before and after photos and a metal check. Ask two lessor technical reps for introductions, since they carry the bigger volume.

title: Retraining-Backed Severance for AI Layoffs
one_liner: Employers replace resume-coaching outplacement with prepaid seats in shortage-role training plus a guaranteed interview pipeline, priced per re-employed worker.
customer: HR and people-ops leaders at 500-20,000 person employers doing AI-related restructuring; hiring employers in healthcare and trades pay placement fees.
problem: Employment of 22-25 year-olds in AI-exposed jobs is 19% below trend and recent grads are 42% underemployed. About half the earnings loss comes from landing in restaurants and retail. Traditional outplacement coaches people back toward the same shrinking roles.
solution: Displaced workers choose from vetted 8-16 week programs into shortage jobs (medical assistant, EMT, CDL, electrician pre-apprenticeship, revenue-cycle, dental support). The employer funds tuition and a stipend from severance budget. Hiring partners guarantee interviews. Use Workforce Pell where a program is approved. Success fee at 90-day retention.
why_now: AI-linked layoffs are drawing PR and political pressure. Workforce Pell has only 5 approved programs, so employer-funded pathways are the fast lane. Employers in experience-rated unemployment-insurance states may also gain from faster re-employment (verify by state).
revenue_model: $4-9k per participant paid by the employer, replacing a $3-5k outplacement fee, plus $1-3k placement fees from hiring partners.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume laid-off white-collar workers should look for adjacent white-collar roles. Those roles are the ones disappearing. Severance is already budgeted money, so converting a slice into a retraining voucher aimed at shortage roles costs the employer little and buys reputation.
first_30_days: Build 3 vetted pathways with local providers in one metro. Pitch 20 HR heads at companies that recently announced cuts. Run a single 25-person pilot and collect 90-day placement outcomes for references.

title: Kin Circles: Chosen-Family Covenants for Solo Agers
one_liner: A structured program where 6-8 unrelated adults form a witnessed, legally backed chosen-family circle that covers emergencies, hospital discharge and funerals.
customer: Adults aged 50-75 with no spouse or children (AARP finds about 12% of Americans over 50 age solo, and Census data show 15.2 million adults over 55 are childless), with senior-living operators and hospitals as second-tier buyers.
problem: At crisis moments such as surgery, discharge, dementia and death, solo agers have no designated person who is legally empowered and emotionally committed to show up. Friendships drift because obligations are unspecified, unwitnessed and not legally recognised.
solution: A six-week guided formation of a Kin Circle of 6-8 people. It produces a written covenant of specific mutual obligations (rides after surgery, weekly check-ins, holiday dinners), a legal packet through flat-fee partner attorneys (health-care proxy, HIPAA release, power of attorney, funeral instructions), and a public vow ceremony with witnesses. An annual renewal ritual and a simple escalation ladder (if someone misses two check-ins the circle is pinged) keep it alive.
why_now: Solo aging is a demographic wave: 43% of women aged 75+ live alone, and about 4 in 10 childless older adults live alone. Loneliness is a public-health issue, and 'chosen family' is mainstream. Guardianship abuse headlines have made older adults want plans that keep them out of the court system.
revenue_model: Formation packages of roughly $500-800 per person, membership of about $12 per month, annual renewal rituals at around $150 per circle, and licensing of the program to senior-living operators and hospital discharge teams. Legal work is sold by the attorney at a flat fee, with no fee-splitting.
non_obvious_insight: Marriage works because it bundles vow, witnesses and legal status into an obligation stack, and platonic groups lack all three. Unbundle that stack and rebuild it for a group; six to eight people share the load so no one burns out, unlike a single friend or a single adult child.
first_30_days: Recruit three pilot circles through community centers, Meetup and solo-aging forums. Sign two estate-planning attorneys for a flat-fee legal packet. Host the first witnessed 'vow night' and film it for testimonials.
